title: Commutes Sentence of Irving Stitsky
description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Irving Stitsky as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: Trump commuted Irving Stitsky’s federal sentence on December 23, 2020. The Justice Department lists an original term of 85 years in prison, three years of supervised release and $23,152,235 in restitution for securities, wire and mail fraud convictions in the Southern District of New York. The clemency register records the grant, but not its full terms.
description_long:
On December 23, 2020, Donald Trump commuted Irving Stitsky’s federal sentence. The Justice Department lists an original judgment from the Southern District of New York: 85 years in prison, three years of supervised release and $23,152,235 in restitution. The offenses included securities fraud, wire fraud and mail fraud. The restitution award was part of the judgment alongside the prison term, so clemency should not be read as erasing the underlying financial obligation.

A commutation grants relief from punishment while leaving the conviction in place; it is different from a pardon. The public clemency register records the original sentence and the date of Trump’s action, but does not show the exact replacement terms in the warrant. It therefore does not establish how much of the prison term was removed or whether any conditions were changed. The documented event is the presidential commutation of a sentence imposed in a securities-fraud case, with the conviction and restitution amount still listed in the federal record.

preserved_fields.title: Commutes Sentence of Irving Stitsky
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Irving Stitsky as part of a clemency list.

title: Commutes Sentence of Jeff Cheney
description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Jeff Cheney as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: Trump commuted Jeff Cheney’s federal sentence on January 19, 2021. Cheney had received 216 months in prison and ten years of supervised release for conspiring to manufacture and distribute methamphetamine after a prior felony drug conviction. The Justice Department’s clemency register identifies the case in Iowa and records the original judgment, but does not specify the revised sentence.
description_long:
Jeff Cheney’s federal case involved a conspiracy to manufacture and distribute at least 500 grams of methamphetamine after a prior felony drug conviction. In 2008, the Northern District of Iowa sentenced him to 216 months in prison and ten years of supervised release. Donald Trump commuted that sentence on January 19, 2021, the day before leaving office.

The Justice Department lists the original punishment and the commutation date, but its public entry does not state what sentence replaced the 216-month term. A commutation changes the punishment; it does not vacate the conviction or amount to an acquittal. The distinction matters here because the record documents relief from the sentence imposed for the drug conspiracy, while leaving the conviction itself in place. The entry also does not explain the clemency decision or specify any revised supervision requirements. Without the warrant’s terms, it is not possible to say how much prison time remained or whether other conditions changed. The established event is the commutation of Cheney’s federal sentence, not a reversal of his case.

preserved_fields.title: Commutes Sentence of Jeff Cheney
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Jeff Cheney as part of a clemency list.

title: Commutes Sentence of Kenneth Charles Fragoso
description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Kenneth Charles Fragoso as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: Trump commuted Kenneth Charles Fragoso’s federal sentence on January 19, 2021. Fragoso had been sentenced to life in prison plus ten years of supervised release for conspiring to possess and distribute more than five kilograms of cocaine. The Justice Department lists the case in the Southern District of Texas and records the original punishment, but not the replacement terms.
description_long:
Kenneth Charles Fragoso was convicted in the Southern District of Texas of conspiring to possess with intent to distribute more than five kilograms of cocaine. The Justice Department records his original sentence as life imprisonment followed by ten years of supervised release. Donald Trump commuted the sentence on January 19, 2021.

The life term makes the clemency action consequential: it granted relief from a sentence that otherwise had no fixed release date. The public clemency record, however, lists the sentence that was imposed before the commutation and does not spell out the new term in its summary. It does not say whether the replacement was time served, whether supervised release remained, or whether the warrant changed other conditions. A commutation modifies punishment but does not erase the conviction. The available record therefore establishes that Fragoso received executive clemency and identifies the offense and original judgment; it does not establish the full practical terms of his release or the reason the administration selected his case.

preserved_fields.title: Commutes Sentence of Kenneth Charles Fragoso
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Kenneth Charles Fragoso as part of a clemency list.

title: Commutes Sentence of Bill K. Kapri
description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Bill K. Kapri as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: Trump commuted Bill K. Kapri’s federal sentence on January 19, 2021. The Southern District of Florida had sentenced Kapri to 46 months in prison and three years of supervised release for two false-statement counts involving the acquisition or attempted acquisition of a firearm. The public clemency listing confirms the grant and original sentence; it does not give the warrant’s revised terms.
description_long:
Bill K. Kapri’s federal conviction involved two false statements made in connection with acquiring or attempting to acquire a firearm. The Southern District of Florida sentenced him to 46 months in prison and three years of supervised release in November 2019. On January 19, 2021, Donald Trump commuted that sentence.

The Justice Department’s clemency record preserves the original offense and punishment, making clear what the executive action changed: Kapri received relief from the sentence for the firearm-related false statements. A commutation is not the same as a pardon and does not set aside a conviction. The public listing does not state what term replaced the 46 months or whether the three years of supervision were altered. It also gives no explanation for the choice of case. Those details require the clemency warrant; they cannot be determined from the date of the grant alone. The documented event is a sentence commutation, not an exoneration or a finding that the conviction was invalid.

title: Commutes Sentence of Mary Anne Locke
description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Mary Anne Locke as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: Trump commuted Mary Anne Locke’s federal sentence on January 19, 2021. Locke had received 234 months in prison and ten years of supervised release for methamphetamine-distribution and money-laundering conspiracies; the drug offense involved activity near a protected location. The Justice Department lists the original judgment in Iowa but does not provide the replacement terms in its public entry.
description_long:
Mary Anne Locke was sentenced in the Northern District of Iowa to 234 months in prison and ten years of supervised release. The Justice Department’s record describes convictions for conspiring to distribute at least 500 grams of methamphetamine within 1,000 feet of a protected location and conspiring to commit money laundering. Donald Trump commuted her sentence on January 19, 2021.

The case combined a drug-distribution offense tied to a protected location with a financial offense, and the original judgment included a lengthy prison term followed by supervision. The commutation granted executive relief from that punishment, but the public listing does not identify the sentence that replaced it or say whether supervision conditions changed. A commutation leaves the conviction in place; it does not reverse the court’s findings. The entry also gives no reason for the grant. Without the warrant, the record cannot establish how the clemency affected Locke’s remaining custody or the conditions that followed. What it does establish is the date of the commutation, the offenses, and the original sentence.

A commutation reduces or changes punishment; it does not itself erase the convictions. The entry therefore documents executive relief in a case with numerous fraud and obstruction counts, while leaving the specific scope of that relief to the warrant. title: Commutes Sentence of Lerna Lea Paulson

The District of North Dakota had sentenced her to 204 months in prison and five years of supervised release for conspiring to possess with intent to distribute and distribute a controlled substance. description_long:
Lerna Lea Paulson received a 204-month prison sentence and five years of supervised release in the District of North Dakota. The Justice Department identifies the conviction as conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute and distribute a controlled substance. Donald Trump commuted her sentence on January 19, 2021.

The commutation came near the end of Trump’s term and changed the punishment attached to Paulson’s federal conviction. The Justice Department’s listing confirms the clemency action and preserves the original sentence, but it does not describe the revised term or say whether supervised release continued under the same conditions. A commutation is a form of sentence relief, not a pardon: it does not vacate the conviction. The public entry also does not explain why Paulson’s case was selected. The signed warrant would be needed to determine the precise scope of the relief. Based on the published record, the supported account is that a federal drug-conspiracy sentence was commuted, while the original conviction remained on the record.

title: Commutes Sentence of Mary Marcella Roberts

Roberts had received 228 months in prison and ten years of supervised release for conspiring to possess with intent to distribute and distribute a controlled substance. The Justice Department’s public record identifies the North Dakota case and original punishment, but does not specify the revised sentence or supervision terms.
description_long:
Mary Marcella Roberts was sentenced in the District of North Dakota to 228 months in prison and ten years of supervised release for a controlled-substance distribution conspiracy. The Justice Department lists the judgment as entered in 2011. Donald Trump commuted her sentence on January 19, 2021.

The published clemency entry documents a change to Roberts’s punishment but does not provide the new sentence in its summary. That distinction matters: a commutation is not an acquittal and does not erase the conviction. The source records the original term and grant date, but a reader cannot tell from that listing alone how much time remained in custody, whether the supervision period changed, or what conditions applied after release. Those specifics are set by the clemency warrant. The event is therefore a presidential decision to reduce or alter a federal sentence for a drug-conspiracy conviction, with the practical scope of the relief left to the signed terms. No additional claim about the case or its outcome follows from the grant itself.

title: Meta Announces Trump Account Reinstatement
description_short: Meta said it would restore Trump’s Facebook and Instagram accounts after the two-year suspension.
description_medium: Meta announced on January 25, 2023, that Donald Trump’s Facebook and Instagram accounts would be restored after a two-year suspension imposed following the January 6 attack on the Capitol. Meta said the suspension period had elapsed and that Trump would again be subject to its platform rules, including heightened penalties for repeat violations.
description_long:
Meta suspended Donald Trump’s Facebook and Instagram accounts after the January 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol, citing the risk of further incitement. The company initially left the suspension’s duration open. In June 2021, it set a two-year period and said it would review whether the danger to public safety had diminished. On January 25, 2023, Meta announced that Trump would be allowed back on both platforms in the coming weeks.

Meta’s president of global affairs, Nick Clegg, said the company wanted the public to hear from elected officials, while also describing the original suspension as an extraordinary step taken in extraordinary circumstances. The reinstatement came with heightened penalties for repeat violations, according to Meta’s announcement. It restored Trump’s ability to publish to two large social networks, but did not exempt his posts from moderation rules. The decision reopened debate about how platforms should handle political speech after a major real-world event, and how long a private company should restrict a public figure’s access.

preserved_fields.title: Meta Announces Trump Account Reinstatement
preserved_fields.description_short: Meta said it would restore Trump’s Facebook and Instagram accounts after the two-year suspension.

title: Trump Pushes 'Delilah Law' to Bar Commercial Licenses for Undocumented Immigrants
description_short: Trump asked Congress to pass the Delilah Law banning commercial licenses for undocumented immigrants.
description_medium: During his February 25, 2026, State of the Union address, Trump asked Congress to pass the “Delilah Law,” a proposal to bar people in the country without legal status from obtaining commercial driver’s licenses. NPR described the measure as one of a small number of specific requests he made to lawmakers. The proposal was not an enacted law.
description_long:
Trump used his February 25, 2026, State of the Union address to ask Congress to pass the “Delilah Law,” which NPR described as a ban on commercial driver’s licenses for people in the country without legal status. The request appeared among a short list of specific measures he asked lawmakers to take up, alongside proposals on drug prices, congressional stock trading and proof of citizenship for voting.

The speech was a request for legislation, not a change to licensing rules already in effect. Congress would have to act before the proposal could become law, and the available account does not set out bill text, sponsors, an enforcement process or a vote schedule. It therefore establishes the policy Trump advocated and the group it would affect, but not how a ban would operate or whether lawmakers would adopt it. The distinction matters because a presidential address can announce priorities without creating a new legal restriction on its own.

preserved_fields.title: Trump Pushes 'Delilah Law' to Bar Commercial Licenses for Undocumented Immigrants
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump asked Congress to pass the Delilah Law banning commercial licenses for undocumented immigrants.

title: Orders Closure of PLO Office in Washington
description_short: The State Department ordered the Palestine Liberation Organization office in Washington, D.C. to close.
description_medium: On September 10, 2018, the State Department ordered the Palestine Liberation Organization’s Washington office to close. The office gave Palestinian representatives an official presence in the U.S. capital. The order ended that channel of representation, but its legal basis, conditions, and the PLO’s response are not established here.
description_long: The State Department ordered the Palestine Liberation Organization’s office in Washington, D.C., to close on September 10, 2018. The office provided Palestinian representatives with an official presence in the U.S. capital and a channel for engagement with U.S. officials. Its closure ended that particular office, but does not by itself establish that all contact between the United States and the PLO stopped. The decision was a discrete change to Palestinian representation in Washington. The reasons for the order, any conditions for reopening, and the PLO’s response are not included in the account of the closure.

title: New York Civil Fraud Trial Begins
description_short: Trump’s civil fraud trial in New York began over allegations of inflating asset values.
description_medium: Trump’s New York civil fraud trial began on October 2, 2023. The state attorney general alleged that Trump and his business inflated asset values in financial statements used in business dealings. The case concerned civil liability and possible remedies, not a criminal conviction. The defendants disputed the allegations as the trial opened.
description_long:
The civil fraud trial brought New York Attorney General Letitia James’s case against Donald Trump and related business defendants into court on October 2, 2023. The state alleged that financial statements overstated the value of Trump Organization properties and other assets. Those valuations, the state argued, mattered to lenders and insurers that relied on the statements in business transactions. Trump and the other defendants disputed the allegations.

Opening the trial moved the case from pretrial litigation into the presentation of evidence. It did not itself establish that any statement was fraudulent or decide what remedies might follow. Because the attorney general brought a civil action, the questions concerned liability under state law and potential civil penalties, rather than criminal guilt or imprisonment. The case put the company’s financial disclosures and valuation practices under judicial scrutiny. Any judgment about particular valuations or the defendants’ responsibility depends on the court’s findings, not simply on the fact that the trial began.

preserved_fields.title: New York Civil Fraud Trial Begins
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump’s civil fraud trial in New York began over allegations of inflating asset values.

title: Targets Sanctuary Cities and Interior Enforcement
description_short: Signed Executive Order 13768 expanding interior enforcement and threatening federal funding for sanctuary jurisdictions.
description_medium: On January 25, 2017, Trump signed Executive Order 13768, “Enhancing Public Safety in the Interior of the United States.” It broadened immigration enforcement priorities and threatened federal funding for jurisdictions that limited cooperation with federal immigration authorities. The order put sanctuary-city policies in direct conflict with the administration’s enforcement agenda.
description_long:
Executive Order 13768 directed federal agencies to broaden immigration enforcement inside the United States and identified jurisdictions that limited cooperation with federal immigration authorities as targets for possible funding restrictions. Trump signed the order on January 25, 2017. It also set out enforcement priorities that reached beyond people convicted of serious crimes, expanding the range of noncitizens identified for removal.

The directive placed pressure on local governments that limited how their employees assisted federal immigration enforcement. Its funding provision did not itself resolve whether the executive branch could withhold particular grants; that question depended on statutory authority and later legal challenges. The order marked an early effort by the administration to tie federal resources to local cooperation on immigration. It established the administration’s policy and threatened consequences for sanctuary jurisdictions, while leaving implementation and the legality of specific funding actions to subsequent decisions.

preserved_fields.title: Targets Sanctuary Cities and Interior Enforcement
preserved_fields.description_short: Signed Executive Order 13768 expanding interior enforcement and threatening federal funding for sanctuary jurisdictions.

title: Creates Schedule F to Purge Civil Service
description_short: Trump signed Executive Order 13957 creating “Schedule F,” enabling mass reclassification of civil servants.
description_medium: Trump created Schedule F through Executive Order 13957 on October 21, 2020. The new category covered federal positions involving confidential or policy-related work and gave agencies a path to reclassify some career employees. Reclassification could reduce the job protections normally attached to those civil-service posts; the order did not itself identify how many employees would be moved.
description_long:
Executive Order 13957 created Schedule F within the federal excepted service. It covered positions the administration considered confidential, policy-determining, policy-making or policy-advocating, and directed agencies to identify roles that fit those criteria. Moving a career position into the category could reduce the protections that ordinarily make civil servants less vulnerable to political dismissal.

Trump signed the order on October 21, 2020, near the end of his first term. The order authorized agencies to begin reviewing positions, but it did not name employees or show how many reclassifications were completed before the next administration took office. The policy raised concerns that a broad interpretation of “policy-related” work could bring career staff under greater political control. Schedule F was therefore a personnel mechanism with potential consequences for the independence of the civil service; its actual reach depended on agency implementation, not on the order’s creation alone.

preserved_fields.title: Creates Schedule F to Purge Civil Service
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump signed Executive Order 13957 creating “Schedule F,” enabling mass reclassification of civil servants.

title: Commutes Sentence of Alice Johnson
description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Alice Marie Johnson after advocacy by Kim Kardashian West.
description_medium: Trump commuted Alice Marie Johnson’s federal life sentence on June 6, 2018, after Kim Kardashian West publicly advocated for her case. Johnson had been serving a life term, and the commutation reduced her punishment. A commutation changes a sentence without vacating the conviction; the public clemency record does not state the administration’s reasons for selecting her case.
description_long:
Alice Marie Johnson was serving a federal life sentence when Donald Trump commuted her sentence on June 6, 2018. Kim Kardashian West had brought public attention to Johnson’s case through advocacy, connecting a high-profile campaign to an individual clemency decision. The commutation reduced Johnson’s punishment but did not erase her conviction.

Presidential commutations can shorten or otherwise alter a federal sentence while leaving the judgment in place. That makes the action distinct from a pardon. The Justice Department’s clemency record documents the grant, while the public account available here does not state the exact revised sentence or describe the administration’s decision process. The event became notable both for the relief granted to Johnson and for the role a prominent outside advocate played in bringing her case to the president’s attention. The record supports that connection in timing and public advocacy, but does not show that celebrity involvement was a formal criterion or explain how similar requests were assessed.

preserved_fields.title: Commutes Sentence of Alice Johnson
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Alice Marie Johnson after advocacy by Kim Kardashian West.

title: Disbands Voter Fraud Commission After Data Grab
description_short: Trump terminated the Presidential Advisory Commission on Election Integrity after controversy over data requests.
description_medium: Trump terminated the Presidential Advisory Commission on Election Integrity on January 3, 2018, after its requests for voter-registration data drew objections from states. The panel had been created to examine claims of voter fraud, but it ended before issuing a final report. Its closure left the commission’s proposed inquiry without a public conclusion from the panel.
description_long:
The Presidential Advisory Commission on Election Integrity was created to examine claims of voter fraud. It requested detailed voter-registration information from states, prompting objections over the scale of the data collection and how the information would be used. Several states resisted the requests. Trump terminated the commission on January 3, 2018, before it issued a final report.

Vice President Mike Pence chaired the panel, with Kansas Secretary of State Kris Kobach as vice chair. Ending the commission halted its planned review, but the closure did not establish whether the underlying claims of widespread fraud were true or false. A commission formed to investigate allegations is not itself evidence that those allegations occurred. Its data requests became a separate source of controversy, raising privacy and federal-authority questions before the panel completed its work. The termination ended this particular federal inquiry without a public set of findings from the commission.

preserved_fields.title: Disbands Voter Fraud Commission After Data Grab
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump terminated the Presidential Advisory Commission on Election Integrity after controversy over data requests.

title: Pardons Michael Behenna
description_short: Trump pardoned former Army officer Michael Behenna, convicted in a 2008 Iraq killing case.
description_medium: Trump pardoned former Army officer Michael Behenna on May 6, 2019, after Behenna was convicted by court-martial of unpremeditated murder and assault arising from a 2008 killing in Iraq. The Justice Department lists an original 25-year confinement term, later reduced to 20 years, and dismissal from service. A pardon is distinct from a sentence commutation.
description_long:
Michael Behenna, a former Army officer, was convicted by court-martial of unpremeditated murder and assault in connection with a 2008 killing in Iraq. The Justice Department records that the military court initially imposed 25 years of confinement, later reduced to 20 years, along with dismissal from service and forfeiture of pay and allowances. Donald Trump granted Behenna a pardon on May 6, 2019.

The pardon came after the military justice system had reviewed the conviction and modified the sentence. It was a presidential act of clemency, not a new trial or an appellate ruling. A pardon forgives the offense; a commutation changes punishment without the same form of forgiveness. The public clemency record confirms the grant and summarizes the original military sentence, but it does not give the president’s full rationale. The event joined presidential clemency to a military murder case while leaving the court-martial history in the record.

preserved_fields.title: Pardons Michael Behenna
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump pardoned former Army officer Michael Behenna, convicted in a 2008 Iraq killing case.

title: Imposes Aluminum Tariffs Under Section 232
description_short: Trump issued Proclamation 9704 imposing 10 percent tariffs on aluminum imports under Section 232.
description_medium: On March 8, 2018, Trump issued Proclamation 9704, imposing a 10 percent tariff on aluminum imports under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act. The administration invoked national security as its legal basis. The measure became part of a wider dispute over steel and aluminum imports and trade policy.
description_long:
Proclamation 9704 imposed a 10 percent tariff on covered aluminum imports after a Commerce Department investigation under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act. The administration said rising imports threatened national security, and Trump signed the measure on March 8, 2018. The tariff applied at the border to covered products, adding a cost for importers of aluminum used in construction, vehicles, packaging and other manufacturing.

Section 232 allows the president to adjust imports after a national-security investigation. Using it for aluminum made the tariff part of a wider debate over whether trade restrictions should serve as an economic or security tool. Importers pay the duty, while the amount passed along to manufacturers and buyers depends on supply chains and market conditions. The proclamation set the rate and the administration’s stated rationale; it did not itself establish what consumers would ultimately pay. The event was the use of a security statute to tax covered aluminum imports, with the broader economic effect depending on how businesses responded.

preserved_fields.title: Imposes Aluminum Tariffs Under Section 232
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump issued Proclamation 9704 imposing 10 percent tariffs on aluminum imports under Section 232.

title: Trump's Pre-Strike Tempo Continued to Outrun Broader Institutional Feedback
description_short: Trump's Pre-Strike Tempo Continued to Outrun Broader Institutional Feedback
description_medium: AP’s linked reconstruction follows the path from doubts about nuclear negotiations to Trump’s order to strike Iran, including the flight on Air Force One. The supplied notes characterize the decision tempo as faster than institutional feedback, but do not identify who reviewed the plan or when. That process claim therefore remains unverified. The report’s chronology needs to be tied to specific briefings before the feedback gap can be described as fact.
description_long: The AP report is titled “From doubts about nuke talks to an Air Force One flight, what led up to Trump's order to strike Iran.” The supplied notes interpret its chronology as showing that Trump’s decision moved faster than institutional feedback. They do not name the officials who reviewed the strike plan, identify what advice they gave, or establish when that advice reached the president. Without those details, the claim about a feedback gap cannot be separated from the writer’s interpretation of the sequence. The available material supports only that AP reconstructed a chain of events leading to the strike order, beginning with doubts about nuclear negotiations and including an Air Force One flight. To assess the stronger process claim, the record needs the article’s specific briefing timeline, the participants and the decisions under review. It also needs evidence for the asserted connection between timing and decision blind spots. The linked article was not accessible during this review, so those particulars remain unresolved rather than being filled in by inference.

title: Trump's Narrative Pivot Space Stayed Constrained in NPR's Evidence-First Coverage
description_short: Trump's Narrative Pivot Space Stayed Constrained in NPR's Evidence-First Coverage
description_medium: NPR reported that records tied to allegations about Trump were absent from the Justice Department’s public Epstein-files database. description_long: On September 10, 2018, the State Department ordered the Palestine Liberation Organization’s Washington, D.C., office to close. The office gave Palestinian representatives an official presence in the U.S. capital and a channel for engagement with U.S. officials. The order addressed that office; it does not, by itself, show that all U.S.–PLO contacts ended or that the organization ceased operating elsewhere. The closure changed the institutional setting for Palestinian representation in Washington. The available account does not explain which legal authority the department relied on, whether the PLO could satisfy conditions to reopen the office, or how the organization responded. Those details affect how the action should be understood: a closure order can rest on statutory, diplomatic or administrative grounds, and its consequences depend on the terms and later decisions. Without the text of the order or a fuller account of the exchange, the reason for the closure and the route to restoring the office remain unclear. The supported facts are the date, the department’s directive and the office it targeted.
